draft.title: Orbital motion
card: A satellite in a circular orbit is always accelerating towards the centre. Gravity from the central mass is the only force providing this centripetal force.
Set the two equal: GMm/r² = mv²/r. The satellite's mass m cancels, so v = √(GM/r).
Here M is the mass being orbited and r is the distance from its centre. Orbital speed depends only on M and r, not on the satellite's own mass.
A larger orbital radius gives a smaller speed. Two satellites at the same radius around the same planet move at the same speed, even if their masses differ.
draft.remember: Gravity is the centripetal force, so v = √(GM/r): only M and r matter.

a.q: Two satellites orbit Earth at the same radius. One has twice the mass of the other. How do their orbital speeds compare?
opts: The heavier one is twice as fast
a.why: Gravity provides the centripetal force, and the satellite's mass cancels from both sides of the equation. Speed depends only on Earth's mass and the orbital radius, so both move at the same speed. A heavier satellite feels more gravity, but it also needs more force to turn, so the effects cancel.
a.clue: What happens to m when you set GMm/r² equal to mv²/r?

b.q: Satellite X orbits a planet at radius r. Satellite Y orbits the same planet at radius 4r. What is the ratio of the speed of Y to the speed of X?
b.why: Speed is v = √(GM/r), so speed is proportional to 1/√r. Radius 4 times larger gives a speed half as large, so Y to X is 1 : 2. The tempting 1 : 4 forgets the square root.
b.clue: Speed depends on the square root of 1/r.
